factious.definition: given to internal conflict and division
sentences: The factious committee split over a font and never reassembled.
A factious party loses to a dull united one every single time.
The outrage was factitious, organized by three accounts and a scheduling tool.
Factitious is manufactured; fictitious is invented. Both are lies with different jobs.
The diet was a fad in 1994, a joke in 1999, and a cookbook again in 2019.
Every fad is a tradition that failed its second year.
The argument was fallacious in a way that took three pages to explain and one line to feel.
A fallacious premise produces a confident, useless conclusion.

fallacy.definition: a mistaken belief or flawed argument
sentences: The sunk-cost fallacy has kept more bad projects alive than any budget.
Naming a fallacy in Latin does not win the argument, though people try.
Memory is fallible in ways that are systematic, which is worse than being random.
A fallible expert who says so is worth two confident ones.
He lay fallow for two years and came back with the best work of his life.
Fields left fallow recover nitrogen; people left fallow recover everything else.
Her voice faltered once, on a name, and then held for the rest of the eulogy.
The campaign faltered in October and collapsed in November.
Fanatical attention to detail built the bridge and ruined four marriages.
A fanatical follower is a liability disguised as an asset.
The fanciful proposal involved a monorail and no visible funding.
Her fanciful drawings of machines predate three of the actual inventions.

fancy.definition: to imagine or take a liking to
sentences: He fancied himself a natural leader, which nobody else fancied at all.
Fancy is a shortened "fantasy," which explains why it means both imagining and liking.

fanfare.definition: a showy public display or flourish
sentences: The product launched with enormous fanfare and was discontinued without a word.
A trumpet fanfare announces the arrival of someone who could have simply knocked.

fare.definition: to get along or turn out in a specified way
sentences: The smaller firms fared better in the crisis because they had less to lose.
How did you fare? is the polite version of what went wrong.

fastidious.definition: very attentive to detail; hard to please
sentences: A fastidious proofreader is worth more to a book than a second author.
He was fastidious about his shoes and cheerfully vague about his taxes.
Nobody could fathom why the timetable had been designed that way.
A fathom measures the depth of water; the verb measures the depth of a mystery.
His fatuous grin survived a question that should have removed it.
A fatuous remark is stupid and pleased with itself, which is the worst combination.
Three deputies fawned over the visitor and one asked a real question.
Dogs fawn honestly; people fawn with an agenda.

fawning.definition: flattering in an excessive, servile way
sentences: The fawning introduction lasted so long the speaker looked embarrassed.
Fawning praise from a subordinate tells you nothing except who is afraid.
The plan was feasible on paper and impossible in February.
Feasible does not mean wise; it only means the physics allows it.
The feckless heir spent four years and the entire estate proving the will right.
Feck is an old word for effect: feckless means, precisely, without effect.
A fecund decade produced nine novels, four of them good.
The delta's fecund soil supported a city for three thousand years.
A feeble excuse delivered confidently often outperforms a good one mumbled.
The signal was too feeble to carry past the second floor.
He feigned surprise so badly that even the cat looked skeptical.
She feigned illness on the day of the exam and caught a real one that evening.

feint.definition: a deceptive move to distract an opponent
sentences: The feint drew defenders left, and the pass went right.
Feint is a fake move; faint is falling over. Boxers do both.
A felicitous phrase in the opening carried the whole essay.
Their meeting was felicitous: two problems that turned out to be each other's solution.
She described the disaster with a felicity that made everyone laugh guiltily.
Domestic felicity is rarely written about because it makes such dull reading.
The phrase "in one fell swoop" preserves an adjective that means murderous.
A fell wind stripped the orchard in a single night.
She ferreted out the discrepancy from a filing cabinet nobody had opened since 1998.
Ferrets were used to flush rabbits from burrows, which is exactly what the verb does.
His fervent defense of the library persuaded a council that had already decided.
Fervent comes from boiling, which is where most convictions live.
The fervid tone of the letter suggested a grievance older than the subject.
Fervid is fervent with the thermostat broken.
Revolutionary fervor lasted eleven months and one very cold winter.
He argued about punctuation with the fervor others reserve for religion.

fester.definition: to worsen through neglect; to become infected
sentences: The grievance festered for six years because nobody wanted an awkward conversation.
A wound festers quietly and then, all at once, urgently.
He was feted in three cities and audited in a fourth.
They feted the retiring caretaker more warmly than any director before him.
The fetid canal was cleaned in 1908 and named after the man who paid for it.
A fetid atmosphere in an office is rarely about the air.
The opening night was a fiasco: two power cuts and a missing lead actor.
Italian for "bottle," and nobody has satisfactorily explained how it came to mean this.
Fickle audiences abandoned the show between two seasons and returned for the reunion.
Fortune is famously fickle, which is the only fair thing about it.
The translation's fidelity to the original made it almost unreadable in English.
High fidelity meant, originally, that the recording resembled the concert.
He meant it figuratively, which the lawyers found insufficiently reassuring.
A figurative bloodbath sells newspapers; a literal one closes them.

filch.definition: to steal something of small value
sentences: Somebody filched the good stapler and the department never recovered.
He filched a peach and paid for it in guilt for thirty years.

filibuster.definition: prolonged speech used to block a vote
sentences: The filibuster ran twenty-four hours and included a recipe for oyster stew.
A filibuster is a speech whose only purpose is its own length.
He finagled an upgrade by knowing the right name and using it sadly.
She finagled the schedule so that every difficult meeting fell on a Friday.

financial.definition: relating to money and its management
sentences: The financial case was flawless and the human case was never made.
Financial literacy is taught nowhere and required everywhere.

finesse.definition: delicate skill in handling a situation
sentences: She handled the resignation with a finesse that left everyone feeling consulted.
The repair needed finesse; it got a hammer.
The finicky printer refused any paper it had not personally approved.
He was finicky about coffee and indifferent to whether the roof leaked.

firebrand.definition: someone who stirs up trouble or passion
sentences: The firebrand of 1968 became the cautious committee chair of 1991.
Every movement needs one firebrand and about forty people who do the paperwork.
A fissure in the party widened into two parties within a year.
Steam escaped from a fissure the survey had marked as sealed.
Fitful sleep before a flight is worse than none at all.
Progress was fitful: three good months, six silent ones, then a breakthrough.
Attention flagged in the third hour and nobody pretended otherwise.
The same word means to mark something for attention, which is confusing at the end of a long meeting.
A flagrant breach of the rules went unpunished, which taught everyone the actual rule.
Flagrant comes from burning: the offense is on fire in plain view.

flail.definition: to wave about wildly; to struggle ineffectively
sentences: The department flailed for a quarter before anyone admitted the strategy had failed.
He flailed at the wasp and hit the lamp.
She had a flair for defusing meetings that had already caught fire.
Flair is talent that wants to be seen.
His flamboyant style hid an accountant's caution about everything that mattered.
Flamboyant means flaming, which is a fair description of the jacket.

flay.definition: to criticize savagely; to strip skin from
sentences: The review flayed the novel and doubled its sales.
To flay in print is legal; to flay in fact has been illegal for some time.
The fledgling company had four employees and one very optimistic sign.
A fledgling is a bird just able to fly, which is exactly the level of confidence involved.
Tourists were fleeced at the border by a man with an official-looking clipboard.
Fleecing a customer once earns more than serving them badly forever, which is why regulation exists.
A fleeting expression crossed his face and was gone before anyone could name it.
Fleeting fame is at least honest about its schedule.
A flip answer to a grieving relative ended his career in customer service.
He gave a flip reply and spent the afternoon apologizing for it.
The flippant tone of the statement made a small problem into a resignation.
Flippant is funny at the wrong moment, which is the only difference between wit and disaster.
His florid prose took four sentences to open a door.
The florid ceiling has more cherubs than the chapel has seats.
A flotilla of fishing boats rescued more people than the navy did that week.
By dawn a flotilla of kayaks blocked the harbor entrance entirely.

flotsam.definition: floating wreckage; worthless odds and ends
sentences: The beach filled with flotsam, and one intact piano.
Flotsam floats off a wreck; jetsam was thrown overboard on purpose.
He floundered through the first ten minutes and then found his footing entirely.
The project floundered for two years and was declared a pilot.
The garden flourished under total neglect, which was humbling.
He flourished the letter above his head as though it were a verdict.
They flouted the ban so publicly that enforcing it became unavoidable.
Flout is to defy; flaunt is to show off. Flouting the difference is common.
Attendance fluctuated with the weather and nothing else anyone could identify.
Prices fluctuate; the explanations offered for it fluctuate faster.
The discovery was a fluke, which the grant application described as a strategy.
Winning twice is skill; winning once is a fluke with a trophy.
The new ticket machine flummoxed commuters and delighted the taxi drivers outside.
One simple question flummoxed a panel of four experts.
Flummoxed by the form, he left it blank and was approved anyway.
The audience looked flummoxed, which the artist took as a compliment.
Flush with grant money, the lab bought a machine it used twice.
The company was flush in spring and borrowing by autumn.
Flustered by the applause, she forgot the name of her own book.
He never looked flustered, which colleagues found either admirable or inhuman.
The department is in flux, which is the official word for nobody knows who reports to whom.
Everything is in flux, said Heraclitus, and has been reliably quoted ever since.
His foibles were catalogued affectionately in a speech he pretended not to enjoy.
Marriage is largely the negotiation of foibles.
The plot was foiled by a locked door nobody had planned for.
As a noun, a foil is the contrast that makes someone else look brighter.

foist.definition: to impose something unwanted on someone
sentences: The extra duties were foisted on the newest hire, as tradition demanded.
He foisted a forgery on two dealers and a museum before anyone checked the frame.
The pamphlet fomented a strike its author had intended merely to describe.
To foment is to apply heat, which is exactly what agitators do to a grievance.
The charge was fomentation of unrest, based on a speech and a rumor.
Fomentation of dissent is only a crime when the dissent succeeds too slowly.
The foolhardy crossing cost two boats and taught the village a permanent lesson.
Courage weighs the risk; foolhardiness has not looked.
His foppish cuffs concealed a man who could rebuild an engine by hand.
The foppish villain in a costume drama is always the second-best character.

forage.definition: to search widely for food or supplies
sentences: They foraged in the fridge and produced dinner from three unlikely ingredients.
Foraging armies feed themselves and empty the countryside behind them.
He forbore to mention the earlier failure, which everyone noticed him not mentioning.
Forbear with an E is patience; forebear with two is your ancestor.
Her forbearance during the interview was mistaken for agreement.
The bank showed forbearance for one quarter and then showed the door.

ford.definition: to cross a river at a shallow point
sentences: They forded the river at dawn and lost only one bag to the current.
Oxford and Frankfurt are both named for places somebody once forded.
Her forebears arrived with one trunk and left an entire street.
We inherit our forebears' habits more reliably than their money.

foreboding.definition: a feeling that something bad will happen
sentences: A sense of foreboding hung over the meeting before a word was spoken.
Foreboding is anxiety that turns out, sometimes, to have been information.
The failure was foreseeable, and two memos had in fact foreseen it.
For the foreseeable future means until somebody changes their mind.

foreshadow.definition: to hint at something that will happen
sentences: The broken clock in chapter one foreshadows everything, as broken clocks do.
Small delays foreshadowed a collapse nobody wanted to name.
A frank memo forestalled a rumor that would have taken months to correct.
To forestall is to get to the market before the seller, which is where the word began.

forfeit.definition: to lose or give up as a penalty
sentences: He forfeited the deposit rather than spend another night in the flat.
The team forfeited the match and won the argument.
A forlorn umbrella stood in the corner for eight months awaiting its owner.
A forlorn hope was originally the first troops into a breach, which explains the tone.
A formal complaint changes everything; an informal grumble changes nothing.
The formal apology was drafted by lawyers and read exactly like it.

formidable.definition: inspiring fear or respect through power
sentences: A formidable opponent in debate, she prepared for arguments nobody had thought to make.
The formidable wall kept out invaders for four centuries and one afternoon.
He forsook a comfortable career for a boat that leaked from the first day.
Wedding vows use forsake because abandon sounds too much like what actually happens.

forswear.definition: to renounce or give up solemnly
sentences: She forswore social media in January and returned, quietly, in March.
He forswore alcohol, sugar, and opinions, and kept two of the three.
Diplomacy was never his forte, which the ambassadorship exposed within a week.
Punctuality is not her forte and never has been, cheerfully.

forthcoming.definition: willing to share information; about to happen
sentences: The witness was less forthcoming after the second cup of coffee, not more.
The forthcoming report has been forthcoming for two years.
His forthright assessment of the budget cost him a friend and saved a department.
Forthright answers make short meetings, which is why they are so rare.

fortify.definition: to strengthen against attack or weakness
sentences: They fortified the argument with data and forgot to make it interesting.
Flour is fortified with iron, which is a quiet public-health triumph.
It took fortitude to sit through the review and thank the reviewers afterward.
Fortitude is courage stretched over months rather than minutes.
The meeting was fortuitous: two strangers, one delayed train, one company.
Strictly it means by chance, though it has quietly acquired the good luck.
Small grants fostered work that no committee would ever have approved directly.
The policy fostered exactly the behavior it was written to prevent.
The merger foundered on a disagreement about which logo survived.
The ship foundered within sight of a harbor it could not enter.
A fracas over seating delayed the ceremony and enlivened the photographs.
The fracas lasted ninety seconds and the inquiry lasted nine months.
A fractious coalition governed for eleven months and agreed on nothing but lunch.
Fractious toddlers and fractious committees respond to identical management.
Human frailty, not conspiracy, explains most institutional failure.
The frailty was physical; the stubbornness was entirely intact.

fraud.definition: deliberate deception for gain; an impostor
sentences: The fraud ran for nine years and required only one unopened envelope to unravel.
He was exposed as a fraud by a student who checked a footnote.
The negotiation was fraught with the history nobody wanted to mention.
A fraught silence at dinner is more informative than any argument.
She entered the fray late and ended it in two sentences.
As a verb it means to unravel, which is what tempers do in a fray.
The frenetic final week produced a report nobody could read.
Frenetic activity is often what an organization does instead of deciding.

fresco.definition: a painting made on wet plaster
sentences: A fresco must be finished before the plaster dries, which is why they are so confident.
The fresco survived because someone whitewashed it in 1660 and forgot.
He fretted about a deadline that had, unknown to him, already been moved.
Fretting is planning with all the useful parts removed.

frieze.definition: a decorative horizontal band on a wall
sentences: The frieze shows a procession that took eleven months to carve and nine minutes to walk past.
Half the frieze is in Athens and half in London, which remains a conversation.

fringe.definition: the outer edge; a marginal group
sentences: The idea lived on the fringe for a decade and is now on the syllabus.
Fringe benefits were originally the small extras at the edge of a wage.
The court dismissed the claim as frivolous and charged the filer for the pleasure.
A frivolous purchase on a bad day is cheaper than most therapies.

frontier.definition: the limit of settled or known territory
sentences: The frontier of the field is wherever the funding was last renewed.
Frontier towns had three saloons and no school, which tells you the priorities.

fructify.definition: to bear fruit or become productive
sentences: The partnership took four years to fructify and then produced everything at once.
Investment fructifies slowly, which is why patience outperforms cleverness.
Frugal by habit rather than necessity, she saved a fortune and mentioned it to nobody.
The frugal meal turned out to be the best one of the trip.
His frugality was legendary and, in the end, entirely pointless.
Frugality practiced only in public is called austerity.
A fruitful hour on the phone replaced a month of email.
The collaboration was fruitful for both and pleasant for neither.
Bad weather frustrated an attempt that had been three years in planning.
Nothing frustrates a plan like another plan filed on the same day.

fulcrum.definition: the pivot point on which something turns
sentences: The single clause was the fulcrum of the entire negotiation.
Give me a lever and a fulcrum, said Archimedes, and I will move the earth.
He fulminated against the reform for a decade and voted for its successor.
Fulminate is to explode: the word means literally to strike with lightning.
A functionary with a stamp can delay you longer than a minister can help you.
The decision was blamed on a functionary who had followed the rules exactly.
Oil is fungible; a good colleague is not, whatever the org chart implies.
Money is fungible, which is why earmarked funding rarely stays earmarked.
The archive furnished the one document the defense had insisted did not exist.
He furnished the flat with three chairs and a piano.
A furtive glance at the door told everyone what the answer would be.
Furtive shares a root with "thief," which is exactly the manner it describes.
Arguing with the parking algorithm was futile and, briefly, satisfying.
The gesture was futile and made anyway, which is often the point of gestures.

gadfly.definition: a persistent critic who provokes others
sentences: Socrates called himself the gadfly of Athens, and Athens executed the insect.
Every board needs one gadfly and cannot survive two.
The gaffe was minor, the apology was worse, and the clip was permanent.
A political gaffe is when someone accidentally says what they think.
Nobody could gainsay the figures, so they questioned the person who found them.
There is no gainsaying her record, however irritating her manner.

gale.definition: a very strong wind; an outburst
sentences: A gale took the roof, the fence, and the argument about who owned the fence.
The joke produced gales of laughter and one very offended trustee.
He had the gall to ask for a refund on a meal he had finished.
Gall was one of the medieval humors, which is why bitterness and nerve share a word.
The photograph galvanized a public that had ignored four years of reports.
Galvani made a dead frog's leg twitch, and the word has been jolting people ever since.

gambit.definition: a calculated opening move involving risk
sentences: Resigning was a gambit; being accepted was the part he had not planned.
In chess a gambit sacrifices a pawn for position, which is also true of most careers.
Lambs gambol for about three weeks and then discover standing still.
The dog gamboled across the lawn and into the pond it had not seen.

garble.definition: to distort a message so it is unclear
sentences: The transmission was garbled and the order was carried out anyway.
One garbled sentence in the summary reversed the finding entirely.
The garish carpet was chosen deliberately so nobody would linger in the corridor.
Garish under fluorescent light and rather lovely by candle, as it turned out.
The film garnered awards abroad and empty cinemas at home.
She garnered support one conversation at a time and won the vote unanimously.
The garrulous barber added twenty minutes and no information to every haircut.
Garrulous witnesses are a lawyer's nightmare and a journalist's dream.
Asking the fee at the funeral was gauche even by his standards.
Gauche is French for left, which is unfair to half the population.

gaunt.definition: thin and haggard from illness or hardship
sentences: He came back gaunt, cheerful, and unwilling to discuss any of it.
The gaunt outline of the mill against the sky is on every local postcard.
Drivers slowed to gawk, which caused a second accident behind the first.
It is possible to gawk politely, though nobody has managed it yet.
The gawky teenager grew into someone the camera followed around a room.
A gawky first draft can still contain the whole book.

generate.definition: to produce or bring into existence
sentences: The policy generated more paperwork than electricity.
One good question generates ten more, which is how research eats decades.

genesis.definition: the origin or beginning of something
sentences: The genesis of the project was an argument in a corridor about a chart.
Everyone claims to have been present at the genesis of anything successful.
His genial manner disguised the fact that he never conceded anything.
A genial host makes even a bad dinner memorable for the right reasons.
Genteel poverty means good furniture and no heating.
The genteel refusal took four sentences to say no.
The hotel's faded gentility was its entire selling point.
Gentility survives longest in the details nobody can afford to replace.

gentry.definition: people of high social class below nobility
sentences: The local gentry opposed the railway until they saw the compensation.
Country gentry produced most of the naturalists and nearly all of the diaries.

germane.definition: relevant to the matter at hand
sentences: The anecdote was entertaining and not remotely germane.
Germane and german both mean closely related; only one now applies to arguments.

gerrymander.definition: to redraw boundaries for political advantage
sentences: The district was gerrymandered into a shape that resembled a salamander, hence the name.
Gerrymandering lets representatives choose their voters instead of the reverse.
The idea gestated for six years in a notebook nobody else could read.
Let it gestate, said the editor, meaning put it in a drawer until January.

gestation.definition: a period of development before emergence
sentences: The law had a gestation of eleven years and a life of eighteen months.
After a long gestation, the design arrived fully formed and immediately obsolete.
The gibe about his accent was repeated so often it became his nickname.
A gibe is a jab; a jibe is a sailing maneuver, though few now distinguish them.

gird.definition: to prepare oneself for something difficult
sentences: The department girded itself for a review that turned out to be a formality.
Gird your loins is ancient advice meaning tuck in your robe before running.
The gist of forty pages was that nobody knew and everybody was busy.
Give me the gist, she said, and received the whole thing anyway.
Progress was glacial, which in this case meant visible only in photographs years apart.
Her glacial silence at dinner was more effective than any argument.
From three interviews she gleaned one fact that changed the whole story.
Gleaning was the right of the poor to gather what the harvest left behind.
The glib answer satisfied the room and none of the people who checked it.
Glib is what fluent sounds like when nothing is behind it.
He glowered at the vending machine as though it had insulted his family.
She glowered through the entire ceremony and applauded, once, at the end.
A glum silence followed the announcement of the new mandatory workshop.
He looked glum for a week and then bought a boat.
A glut of graduates in one field creates a shortage in another five years later.
The glut of tomatoes ended in nine jars of chutney nobody wanted.
He was goaded into a response that cost him considerably more than silence.
A goad was a spiked stick for driving cattle, which is exactly the manner intended.

goosebumps.definition: bumps on the skin from cold or emotion
sentences: The final chord gave four hundred people goosebumps simultaneously.
Goosebumps are a vestige of fur we no longer have, raising hair that no longer helps.
The evidence was gossamer: suggestive, beautiful, and unable to bear any weight.
Gossamer threads across the field are visible only for an hour after dawn.

gouge.definition: to overcharge; to cut out roughly
sentences: Hotels gouged travelers during the storm and were named in the paper for it.
The flood gouged a channel through what had been the main street.

gradation.definition: a gradual step or shading between stages
sentences: Between the two positions lie forty gradations, and every meeting occupies a different one.
The gradation of color from the horizon upward is the whole point of the painting.

graft.definition: corruption for personal gain; a transplant
sentences: Graft in the contracting office cost the city more than the projects were worth.
The skin graft took, and the scandal did not.
Egypt was the granary of Rome, which explains a great deal of Roman politics.
The granary burned in August, which is the worst possible month for a granary to burn.
The grandiloquent toast lasted eleven minutes and mentioned the couple twice.
Grandiloquent prose is a small idea in a very large coat.

grandstand.definition: to behave showily to impress onlookers
sentences: He grandstanded for the cameras and let the committee do the actual work.
Grandstanding at a hearing is free; governing afterward is not.
Granted, the timing was poor — but the decision was still correct.
The council granted permission and withheld the money, which amounted to refusal.

grapple.definition: to struggle with a problem or opponent
sentences: The essay grapples honestly with a question it never manages to answer.
Two committees grappled with the same problem in separate rooms for a year.
It gratified him enormously that the correction ran on the front page.
Instant gratification is expensive precisely because it is instant.
His grating laugh was audible through two doors and one very thick wall.
The grating cheerfulness of the hold music made the wait longer.
The advice was gratis and worth approximately that.
They offered the venue gratis, which turned out to include a bill for cleaning.
Her gratitude took the form of a letter that the recipient framed.
Gratitude expressed late is still better than gratitude felt silently.
The gratuitous insult in the footnote was the only part anyone quoted.
Gratuitous means both free of charge and uncalled for, which says something.
He failed to grasp the gravity of the situation until the lawyers arrived.
The gravity of his expression was undermined slightly by the party hat.
Gregarious to a fault, he knew everyone's name and nobody's phone number.
Gregarious animals form herds; gregarious people form committees.

grievance.definition: a real or imagined cause for complaint
sentences: The grievance was filed in March and resolved, sort of, in November.
An unaddressed grievance compounds faster than any debt.
A grievous error in the dosage was caught by a pharmacist who happened to look twice.
The loss was grievous and the statement about it was four lines long.
They griped about the coffee for years and organized nothing about the pay.
Griping is complaint with no intention of resolution.
The grisly details were omitted from the report and included in the podcast.
Grisly means horrifying; grizzly is a bear. Meeting the second can produce the first.
He groused about the new system and used it more than anyone else.
Soldiers grouse; when they stop, the officers worry.
Plato taught in a grove, which is why academies still pretend to have gardens.
The olive grove had been in the family since a war nobody could name.
He groveled by email, which is the most excruciating available medium.
Groveling rarely restores what honesty would have preserved.
Grudging respect from a rival is worth more than easy praise from a friend.
The grudging apology managed to blame the carpet.
Oliver Twist asked for more gruel, which tells you how bad the alternative was.
The soup was gruel with ambitions.
A single guffaw from the back row rescued a joke that had died on delivery.
His guffaw could be identified from another floor of the building.
He won the contract by guile and lost the renewal by reputation.
Guile is intelligence with the ethics removed.
Her guileless question exposed the whole scheme in one sentence.
Guileless in a negotiation is either a weakness or a very advanced technique.
The scam targeted the gullible and caught, as usual, the merely busy.
Everyone believes they are the one person too sharp to be gullible.
It took gumption to walk into that office without an appointment and a plan.
She had the gumption to ask and got what forty politer people did not.
The meal was a gustatory event and a financial one.
Gustatory memory outlasts almost every other kind, which is why smell ambushes you.
He attacked the buffet with a gusto the hosts had not budgeted for.
She sang badly and with such gusto that nobody minded.
A gusty afternoon ended the picnic and started a tradition of indoor ones.
Gusty conditions delayed the landing by an hour and the apology by three.
The speech was a chain of hackneyed phrases held together by pauses.
A hackney was a horse for hire, worn out by everyone — hence the word.
They haggled for forty minutes over a sum smaller than the coffee they drank afterward.
In some markets refusing to haggle is the rudest thing you can do.
The paper hailed the discovery as a breakthrough and buried the retraction.
He hailed a taxi and, in the same gesture, ended the argument.
The halcyon days of the department lasted from 1994 to a specific Tuesday in 1997.
The halcyon was said to calm the sea while nesting, which is where the word got its peace.

hale.definition: healthy and robust, especially in old age
sentences: Hale at ninety, he still cycled to the shop for a newspaper he did not read.
Hale and hearty is redundant and has survived anyway.
Understatement was the hallmark of her prose and the despair of her publisher.
Hallmarks were literal stamps applied at Goldsmiths' Hall to certify purity.
His halting delivery made the audience listen harder than any polish would have.
The negotiations resumed in a halting way and stopped again by Thursday.
Fog hampered the search for two days and then lifted, unhelpfully, at dusk.
The investigation was hampered by files that had been filed correctly, once, in 1978.

hamstrung.definition: severely restricted in ability to act
sentences: The agency was hamstrung by a budget that arrived nine months late.
To hamstring is to cut the tendon; the metaphor has not softened.
He had a hankering for the town he had spent his youth escaping.
A hankering for salt at midnight has ended many otherwise sound diets.
The filing was haphazard, which meant everything was findable by exactly one person.
A haphazard search found what a systematic one had missed twice.
The hapless intern was blamed for a decision made three levels above him.
Hapless means without hap, an old word for luck.
The harangue lasted forty minutes and converted precisely nobody.
A harangue differs from a speech mainly in the exits people take during it.

harbinger.definition: a sign of something to come
sentences: The first crocus is a harbinger of spring and, usually, of one more frost.
Falling orders were the harbinger; the closure took another eighteen months.

hardy.definition: tough and able to endure difficult conditions
sentences: The hardy little plant survived a winter that killed everything around it.
A hardy few stayed to the end of the meeting and shaped the entire policy.
The harried waiter took four orders, corrected two, and never once stopped smiling.
A harried expression at the airport is the most universal human experience.
The testimony harrowed a courtroom that had heard a great deal already.
A harrow breaks up soil; the verb does something similar to a person.
The harrowing account was read aloud once and never printed.
A harrowing journey makes for a terrible week and an excellent book.
Creditors harried the firm for a year before anyone senior returned a call.
Light cavalry harried the retreat and did more damage than the battle.
Her haughty dismissal of the question was quoted for a decade.
Haughty comes from "high": the nose is doing the talking.
The hauteur of the concierge suggested the hotel was doing you a favor.
Hauteur is arrogance that has been to finishing school.

haven.definition: a place of safety or refuge
sentences: The reading room was a haven from a building otherwise dedicated to noise.
A tax haven offers a different kind of shelter to a different kind of refugee.
They rushed headlong into a merger that took nine years to unwind.
He fell headlong down the stairs and blamed the carpet, correctly.

headstrong.definition: stubbornly determined to have one's way
sentences: The headstrong young captain ignored the chart and discovered a reef.
Headstrong is admirable in a founder and exhausting in a colleague.
